item.title: Could a Tiny 'Rainbow on a Chip' Supercharge the Internet of Tomorrow?
item.description: Deep inside a laboratory, a chip the size of a grain of rice turns a beam of invisible light into a perfect little rainbow. That tiny spectrum could one day carry far more of the world's data at once.

item.title: How can a laser beam curve like a spinning ping-pong ball?
item.description: A table-tennis spin makes a ball swerve in mid-air. Physicists have just found a matching twist inside a tightly focused laser — and it could matter for quantum computers.

item.title: What Are Bethe Strings, the Quantum Knots Predicted Nearly a Century Ago?
item.description: Back in 1931, physicist Hans Bethe imagined particles that could cling together without any chemical glue — a kind of quantum knot that only works in one dimension. Almost a hundred years later, scientists in Austria have finally made them and watched them collide without breaking apart.

item.title: What Is the Quantum 'Energy Ladder' That Took 40 Years to Measure?
item.description: For four decades, physicists predicted that certain quantum systems should settle into energy steps at very particular spacings — like rungs on a ladder. Now a team at Caltech has finally measured those rungs directly, using atoms held in place by tweezers made of light.

item.title: Did Magnetism Help Build the Solar System 4.6 Billion Years Ago?
item.description: Long before there were planets, a vast cloud of gas and dust collapsed into a spinning disk. Gravity always got the credit — but tiny grains locked inside an icy meteorite suggest a second force was quietly at work.

item.title: What Happened When a Couple Built a Bench for a Girl at Their Driveway Bus Stop?
item.description: Every school morning, a middle schooler waited for her bus at the end of a Florida driveway — sitting on the bare ground with no sidewalk in sight. Two teachers decided that wasn't good enough, and one small wooden bench turned into a whole lot more.

item.title: Was the American 'Cheetah' Really a Cheetah After All?
item.description: Ancient DNA shows the speedy Ice Age cat that once chased North America's pronghorn was actually a puma in disguise.

item.title: Why Are JWST's Mysterious 'Little Red Dots' Secretly Growing Black Holes?
Can Love Find You Again at 88? These Two Retirees Say Yes
item.description: Barbara and Fred both lost their long-time partners — then met among the barbells at their retirement village gym. Now, at 88 and 89, they are proof that a second chance at happiness has no age limit.

item.title: Could Living Bacteria Become the Switches Inside a Computer?
item.description: Engineers at MIT have grown living circuits out of bacteria, turning colonies of microbes into switches that can pass signals along — a computer made of life itself.

item.title: Could a $100 Detector Really See Invisible Particles Falling from Space?
item.description: Tiny particles from space pass through our bodies every second, but a pocket-sized detector built from $100 in parts can catch them — and it's now used by students and scientists around the world.

item.title: What Does a Mysterious Wall in Morocco Reveal About Ancient Africa?
item.description: In the hills of north-west Morocco, an old wall overlooking a river turns out to be roughly 4,000 years old — the earliest confirmed defensive construction in North Africa beyond Egypt, and a sign that the region was anything but a backwater.

item.title: How a £30m Public Appeal Saved Rothbury Estate for Wildlife
How Does Saturn's Icy Moon Make Hidden Clues to Life Easier to Find?
item.description: Enceladus sprays bits of its hidden ocean into space. New lab experiments show the frozen droplets separate their salts on the way up, quietly concentrating the clues scientists hope to find.

item.title: Why Did Crocodiles Survive the Asteroid That Killed the Dinosaurs?
item.description: Sixty-six million years ago an asteroid wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs, yet crocodiles and their ancient relatives lived on. New research suggests the secret was simple: they loved warm weather, and the tropics stayed warm enough to shelter them.

item.title: What Do Quark Wakes Teach Us About the Universe's Primordial Soup?
How Did World Countries Agree to Protect 30% of Earth by 2030?
item.description: At the COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, countries reached a deal to implement the 2022 Global Biodiversity Framework — but the big missing piece is money.

item.title: How Did Scientists Read a 2,000-Year-Old Scroll by Burning a Brand-New One?
item.description: Nearly 2,000 years ago, Mount Vesuvius turned a Roman library into lumps of black charcoal. Now scientists have found a clever trick for peering inside those fragile scrolls — and to test it, they burned some brand-new ones of their own.

item.title: How Did 400,000-Year-Old Teeth Link Early Humans to Us Today?
item.description: Tooth proteins pulled from 400,000-year-old Homo erectus molars are revealing quiet family ties between an early human ancestor, the Denisovans, and some of us alive today.

item.title: How Did One New Skull Fragment Push Homo erectus Back 200,000 Years?
item.description: A dusty box of fossils from a South African cave sat unstudied for decades. Among them was something no one expected: the oldest adult Homo erectus skull piece ever found.
